attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you put numbers between 500 and 2000 in the (pick random) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you find the coordinates of a tile on the tilemap?

❓If you wanted a projectile to appear randomly between every 0.5-5 seconds, what should you put in the (pick random) block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When determining the interval for the [on game update every ms] loop, encourage the ninja to think about what a reasonable pace for the projectile might be so that it is challenging, but not impossible for the Player sprite to avoid the projectiles.
steps.instructions:
Create Projectiles as moving obstacles for the Player sprite to avoid! 


Drag a [place sprite on top of] block into the [on game update every ms] loop and select the [projectile] sprite name. Set the coordinates so that the Projectile appears on the ground and starts on the right side of the screen. 


Drag a (pick random) block into the parameter of the [on game update every ms] container. Set the values so that the Projectile sprites appear at a different time interval, each time the project runs


Click ▶ to see the projectiles appear from the right side and move across the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Player sprite’s velocity y to -200 so it jumps up when the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you find the coordinates of a tile on the tilemap?

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed? 

❓ How does a negative value affect the Player sprite’s velocity y? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡By setting the Player sprite’s [vy (velocity y)] value, the ninja is defining how quickly and in which direction the sprite will move along the y axis, when the A button is pressed. A vy value of -200 will cause the Player sprite to move in an upwards direction. A change in y value causes a sprite to move up or down, whereas a change in x value causes a sprite to move left or right.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to jump over the projectile sprites! 


Drag a [place sprite on top of] block into the [on start] container, and set coordinates so that the Player sprite appears on the ground, in column 1. 


Drag an [on button pressed] container into the editor. Then, add a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on button pressed] container. Select the Player sprite’s name, then click the dropdown and select [vy (velocity y)], then set the parameter to -200. This will allow the sprite to jump up when the A button is pressed.


Click ▶ and press the A button to see the Player sprite jump up!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place a [set sprite [ay (acceleration y)] block in the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should you set the Player sprite’s velocity and acceleration?

❓ By setting the [ay (acceleration y)], will it cause a change in the Player sprite’s movement up and down or left and right?

❓ Why does pressing the A button multiple times cause the Player sprite to jump higher?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 It is necessary to set the Player sprite’s acceleration, so that it returns to the “ground” after it jumps upward on the tilemap. Prompt the ninja to consider what happens in real life when they jump in the air, and why they would want to mirror this action in a game.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! Once the Player sprite jumps up, it does not come back down. 


Drag a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on start] container, select the Player sprite’s name, select [ay (acceleration y)] in the drop down, and type 500 as the parameter. This will create “gravity” that pulls the sprite back to the ground.


Click ▶ then press the A button to see the Player sprite return to the ground after it jumps. Notice how pressing the button multiple times makes the Player sprite jump higher!

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace the <true> value of the [if then] conditional with an <is sprite hitting wall> block and select [bottom]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why would you want the Player sprite to be able to jump only when standing on a wall tile?

❓ How does the <is sprite hitting wall> block act similarly to the <is button pressed> block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Again, prompt the ninja to think about what happens when they try to jump in the air—are they able to jump when not standing on a solid surface? Encourage the ninja to think of any game examples that they know of where a sprite can(not) move upwards when not standing on a solid surface.
steps.instructions:
Pressing the A button repeatedly allows the Player sprite to jump even when it’s not on the ground! Code the Player sprite to only jump if it is standing on the ground. 


Add an [if then] conditional to the [on A button pressed] container. Then, open Scene and replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> block. Select the Player sprite's name, then click the drop down to select [bottom]. 


Place the [set sprite vy (velocity y)] block inside the conditional.


﻿Click ▶ then press the A button to see that the Player sprite is only able to jump when the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the second sprite kind in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container to (Projectile)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What else might happen when the Player sprite overlaps with aProjectile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to think about how projectiles are used as an obstacle in this game. Prompt the ninja to consider how other obstacles or projectiles might be used differently to make the project more interesting.
steps.instructions:
End the game if the Player touches a Projectile! 


Drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container and set the second sprite kind to Projectile. Drag a [game over] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Projectile)] container and set the parameter to <LOSE>. 


Click ▶ to see the game end if the Player sprite touches a Projectile sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the [change variable by] block into the top of the [on game update every ms] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What happens each time a projectile appears on the tilemap?

❓ What does the projectile’s vx value change? How will the changing variable impact it?

❓ What will the projectile’s speed be the second time the [on game update every ms] loop is run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to make a connection between the vx value in the projectile’s [set sprite to] block and how they’ve already set the Player sprite’s vy value. The projectile’s changing vx value will change how quickly the projectile moves from right to left across the screen (due to its negative value).
steps.instructions:
Make the game more challenging by using a variable to increase the speed of the Projectile! 


Add a [set [variable] to] block into the [on start] container. Name the variable [speed], and set the value to -75. Then, drag a [change [variable] by] block into the top of the [on game update every ms] container and set the parameter to -5.


Replace the vx parameter of the [set projectile to] block with a (speed) variable. 


Click ▶ to see the Projectile sprite increase its speed as the Player sprite jumps over more and more Projectiles!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as a score variable, dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Finish this project by adding a score variable and directions with a dialog box.


Drag a [set score to] block into the [on start] container and a [change score by] block into the bottom of the [on game update every ms] loop. This will count how many times a Projectile has moved across the screen (and how many times the Player sprite has jumped over it).


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a platformer project with a 2D tilemap that requires a Player to jump over obstacles!

validationItems.text: Projectile sprites move right to left across the tilemap ground, at random time intervals.
Player sprite is positioned on the left side of tilemap ground, and jumps up when A button is pressed.
Player sprite is pulled back down to the tilemap floor after jumping up.
Player sprite can only jump up when the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Game ends when the Player sprite touches a Projectile sprite.
Projectile sprite’s speed increases with a variable that is changed on each game update.
The score increases with each new Projectile sprite on the screen. Game instructions are shared in a dialog box.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about 2D platformer games and physics. In 2D platformers, we see the game as if looking from the side. We can use physics concepts, like velocity and acceleration, to make our sprites jump up onto platforms and avoid obstacles. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Let’s Get Physics-cal!
badges.description: Use physics to control sprite movement in a platformer-style tilemap project.

badges.title: Hop, Skip, and a Jump
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-velocity (vy).

badges.title: Defying Gravity
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-acceleration (ay).

badges.title: Wallflower
badges.description: Check if a sprite is touching a tilemap wall before making something happen in a project.
